nodes.label: Scientific methods and theories develop over time with new evidence
nodes.objective: Understand that scientific models/theories change as new data emerges.
essentialPoints: Theories are provisional and change when new data emerges
New observations/experiments can support or refute existing models

nodes.label: Using scientific models to explain and predict
nodes.objective: Use representational, spatial, descriptive, computational and mathematical models to explain and predict phenomena.
essentialPoints: Models represent real phenomena to aid explanation and prediction
Models can be tested against experimental/observational data
Models have limitations and can be shown to break down

nodes.label: Power and limitations of science, and ethical issues
nodes.objective: Appreciate that science cannot answer all questions and that some questions raise ethical issues.
essentialPoints: Data may be uncertain, incomplete, or unavailable, limiting what science can answer
Some questions involve ethical judgements science alone cannot resolve

nodes.label: Technological applications of science and their implications
nodes.objective: Explain everyday/technological applications of science and evaluate personal, social, economic and environmental implications.
essentialPoints: Scientific applications have personal, social, economic and environmental consequences
Evaluating an application means weighing these implications using evidence

nodes.label: Evaluating risk in practical science and society
nodes.objective: Evaluate risks in practical science and in wider society, including differences between measured and perceived risk.
essentialPoints: Hazards from science-based technology must be weighed against benefits
Perceived risk can differ from measured risk (e.g. voluntary vs imposed, familiar vs unfamiliar, visible vs invisible)

nodes.label: Peer review and communicating scientific results
nodes.objective: Recognise the role of peer review in validating scientific claims and communicating findings.
essentialPoints: Peer review checks results before publication to detect false claims and build consensus
Media reports of science are not peer reviewed and may be biased, oversimplified or inaccurate

nodes.label: Developing a hypothesis from theory
nodes.objective: Use scientific theories and explanations to develop a testable hypothesis.
essentialPoints: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation derived from existing theory
Hypotheses must be capable of being supported or refuted by evidence

nodes.label: Independent, dependent and control variables
nodes.objective: Identify and distinguish independent, dependent and control variables in an investigation.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is changed/selected by the investigator
Dependent variable is measured for each change in the independent variable
Control variables are kept constant so comparisons are fair

nodes.label: Planning experiments and procedures
nodes.objective: Devise and justify a procedure to test a hypothesis, manipulating and controlling variables appropriately.
essentialPoints: A well-designed procedure controls variables and directly tests the hypothesis
Explaining why a procedure is well designed requires reference to variable control

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate apparatus, techniques and materials
nodes.objective: Apply knowledge of apparatus, techniques and materials to select those appropriate for a given experimental purpose.
essentialPoints: Choice of instrument/apparatus depends on the range and precision needed
Justification requires linking apparatus properties to the purpose of measurement

nodes.label: Health and safety: hazards and risk reduction
nodes.objective: Identify hazards in practical contexts and suggest methods to reduce risk of harm.
essentialPoints: A hazard is a source of potential harm; a risk is the chance of that harm occurring
Practical risks can be reduced by specific precautions (e.g. insulation, eye protection, safe handling)

nodes.label: Sampling techniques for representative data
nodes.objective: Recognise when and how to apply sampling techniques to ensure collected data is representative.
essentialPoints: Sampling is needed when it is impractical to measure an entire population/data set
A representative sample avoids bias in the conclusions drawn

nodes.label: Reading and recording measurements from a scale
nodes.objective: Make and record observations and measurements accurately using a range of apparatus, reading scales correctly.
essentialPoints: Measurements must be read to the resolution of the instrument's scale
Recorded values should include appropriate units and significant figures

nodes.label: Evaluating methods and suggesting improvements
nodes.objective: Evaluate an experimental method for validity and sufficiency of data, suggesting improvements and further investigations.
essentialPoints: Assess whether enough precise measurements were taken to support a conclusion
A valid method tests only the intended variable and controls others properly

nodes.label: Constructing and interpreting tables, bar charts and histograms
nodes.objective: Present observations and data using frequency tables, bar charts and histograms.
essentialPoints: Frequency tables organise raw data into categories or class intervals
Bar charts and histograms visually represent frequency data for interpretation

nodes.label: Plotting two variables from data
nodes.objective: Plot two variables from experimental or other data on a graph with appropriate axes and scales.
essentialPoints: Independent variable is plotted on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis
Axes must be labelled with quantity and unit, with sensible scales

nodes.label: Translating data between graphical and numeric forms
nodes.objective: Convert data between tabular/numeric form and graphical representation.
essentialPoints: Values from a table can be read directly onto a graph and vice versa
Graphical trends can be described in words or numbers

nodes.label: Using appropriate significant figures
nodes.objective: Express calculated and measured values to an appropriate number of significant figures.
essentialPoints: The number of significant figures in an answer should reflect the precision of the data used
Rounding too early or reporting excess figures misrepresents precision

nodes.label: Calculating arithmetic mean and range
nodes.objective: Find the arithmetic mean and range of a set of repeated measurements.
essentialPoints: Mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values
Range is the difference between the largest and smallest value, used as a measure of spread

nodes.label: Understanding mean, mode and median
nodes.objective: Understand and distinguish the statistical terms mean, mode and median.
essentialPoints: Mode is the most frequently occurring value
Median is the middle value when data is ordered

nodes.label: Order of magnitude calculations
nodes.objective: Make order of magnitude estimates and comparisons using powers of ten.
essentialPoints: An order of magnitude estimate rounds a quantity to the nearest power of ten
Comparing orders of magnitude allows quick estimation of scale differences

nodes.label: Changing the subject of an equation
nodes.objective: Rearrange an algebraic equation to make a different quantity the subject.
essentialPoints: Rearranging isolates the required unknown on one side of the equation
The same operation must be applied to both sides to preserve equality

nodes.label: Substituting values into equations with correct units
nodes.objective: Substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using appropriate units for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Each value substituted must be in units consistent with the equation (e.g. SI base units)
The final answer's unit follows from the units of the substituted quantities

nodes.label: Determining slope and intercept of a linear graph
nodes.objective: Determine the gradient and y-intercept of a linear graph and relate them to y = mx + c.
essentialPoints: Gradient is calculated as change in y divided by change in x between two points on the line
The y-intercept is the value of y where the line crosses the y-axis
y = mx + c represents a linear relationship where m is gradient and c is intercept

nodes.label: Using the tangent to a curve to find rate of change
nodes.objective: Draw a tangent to a point on a curve and use its slope to determine an instantaneous rate of change.
essentialPoints: A tangent is a straight line touching a curve at one point without crossing it
The gradient of the tangent equals the instantaneous rate of change at that point

nodes.label: Finding the area between a curve and the x-axis
nodes.objective: Determine the physical significance of the area under a graph and measure it by counting squares.
essentialPoints: The area between a curve and the x-axis can represent a physical quantity (e.g. distance from a velocity-time graph)
Area under a curved graph can be estimated by counting the enclosed squares

nodes.label: Estimating uncertainty using the range about the mean
nodes.objective: Represent distributions of results and estimate uncertainty using the range of measurements about the mean.
essentialPoints: Every measurement has some associated uncertainty
The range of repeated measurements about the mean can be used as an estimate of uncertainty

nodes.label: Interpreting data: patterns, trends, predictions and conclusions
nodes.objective: Interpret data in various forms to identify patterns/trends, make predictions and draw conclusions.
essentialPoints: Patterns and trends in data can be recognised across tabular, graphical and other forms
Conclusions must be drawn directly from, and be limited to, the evidence available

nodes.label: Using scatter diagrams to identify correlation
nodes.objective: Use a scatter diagram to identify whether a correlation exists between two variables.
essentialPoints: A scatter diagram plots pairs of values to reveal a possible relationship
Correlation shown on a scatter diagram does not by itself prove causation

nodes.label: Relating data to hypotheses in reasoned explanations
nodes.objective: Present reasoned explanations relating data back to a hypothesis, comparing competing hypotheses.
essentialPoints: The extent to which data supports a hypothesis must be explicitly justified using the evidence
Where multiple hypotheses exist, the one better supported by the data should be identified with reasons

nodes.label: Accuracy and precision of measurements
nodes.objective: Distinguish accuracy (closeness to true value) from precision (closeness of clustering of repeated measurements).
essentialPoints: An accurate measurement is close to the true value
Measurements are precise if they cluster closely together, regardless of accuracy

nodes.label: Repeatability and reproducibility of measurements
nodes.objective: Distinguish repeatable results (same method/investigator) from reproducible results (different method/investigator).
essentialPoints: Measurements are repeatable if the same investigator repeats the method under the same conditions and gets similar results
Measurements are reproducible if different investigators or different equipment give similar results

nodes.label: Random and systematic error
nodes.objective: Identify potential sources of random and systematic error and explain how each affects results.
essentialPoints: Random error causes results to vary unpredictably and can be reduced by repeating measurements and averaging
Systematic error causes results to differ from the true value by a consistent amount and is not reduced by averaging

nodes.label: Identifying and handling anomalous results
nodes.objective: Recognise anomalous values, investigate their cause, and exclude them if due to poor measurement.
essentialPoints: An anomalous result lies clearly outside the pattern of the rest of the data set
An anomaly should be investigated and, if due to a measurement error, excluded before further analysis

nodes.label: Communicating scientific rationale, methods and conclusions
nodes.objective: Present coherent, logically structured reports of investigations including rationale, method, findings and conclusions.
essentialPoints: A scientific report should logically link rationale, method, results and conclusion
Presentation may use verbal, diagrammatic, graphical, numerical or symbolic forms as appropriate

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary and definitions correctly
nodes.objective: Use correct scientific vocabulary, terminology and definitions in written and spoken explanations.
essentialPoints: Precise scientific terms must be used with their exact accepted meaning
Definitions should be stated using established scientific vocabulary

nodes.label: Scientific quantities and how they are determined
nodes.objective: Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and understand how they are measured or determined.
essentialPoints: A physical quantity consists of a numerical value and a unit
Quantities are determined by defined measurement procedures using appropriate instruments

nodes.label: Using SI units correctly
nodes.objective: Use SI units (e.g. kg, m, J) appropriately for physical quantities.
essentialPoints: Each physical quantity has a standard SI unit (e.g. kilogram for mass, metre for length, joule for energy)
Consistent use of SI units allows valid calculation and comparison

nodes.label: Using prefixes and powers of ten for orders of magnitude
nodes.objective: Use standard prefixes (tera, giga, mega, kilo, centi, milli, micro, nano) to express quantities across orders of magnitude.
essentialPoints: Each prefix corresponds to a specific power of ten multiplier (e.g. kilo = 10^3, milli = 10^-3)
Prefixes allow convenient expression of very large or very small quantities

nodes.label: Interconverting units
nodes.objective: Convert a quantity between different units, including using prefixes and standard form.
essentialPoints: Converting units requires multiplying or dividing by the appropriate conversion factor
Prefix values must be applied consistently when converting between unit sizes

nodes.label: Using standard form for very large or small numbers
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in standard form (a × 10^n).
essentialPoints: Standard form expresses a number as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten
Standard form is used to represent very large or very small physical quantities concisely

nodes.label: Recognising and using decimal form
nodes.objective: Recognise and use expressions in decimal form.
essentialPoints: Decimal form expresses quantities using place value with a decimal point

nodes.label: Using ratios, fractions and percentages
nodes.objective: Use ratios, fractions and percentages to solve numerical problems in physics contexts.
essentialPoints: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind
Percentages and fractions are used to express proportions of a whole, including efficiency-style calculations

nodes.label: Making estimates of the results of calculations
nodes.objective: Make sensible estimates of the results of simple calculations without full computation.
essentialPoints: Estimation uses rounded values to quickly approximate a calculation's result
Estimates allow a check on whether a calculated answer is reasonable

nodes.label: Solving simple algebraic equations
nodes.objective: Solve simple algebraic equations for an unknown quantity.
essentialPoints: Solving an equation isolates the unknown value using valid algebraic steps

nodes.label: Understanding and using mathematical symbols (=, <, >, ∝, ~)
nodes.objective: Understand and correctly use symbols including =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝, ~ in scientific contexts.
essentialPoints: Each symbol has a precise mathematical meaning (e.g. ∝ means 'directly proportional to')
Correct use of these symbols allows concise expression of relationships between quantities

nodes.label: Using angular measures in degrees
nodes.objective: Use angular measures in degrees, including for reflection and refraction contexts.
essentialPoints: Angles are measured in degrees from a specified reference line (e.g. the normal)

nodes.label: Visualising and representing 2D and 3D forms
nodes.objective: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms, including 2D representations of 3D objects, e.g. ray diagrams and field patterns.
essentialPoints: 3D physical situations are often represented using 2D diagrams (e.g. cross-sections, ray diagrams)
Interpreting such diagrams requires understanding the spatial relationships they represent

nodes.label: Calculating areas and volumes of simple shapes
nodes.objective: Calculate areas of triangles and rectangles, and surface areas and volumes of cubes, for use in physics calculations.
essentialPoints: Area of a rectangle = length × width; area of a triangle = ½ × base × height
Volume of a cube = side³; surface area of a cube = 6 × side²

nodes.label: AT1: Using measuring cylinders, thermometers, and length instruments
nodes.objective: Use rulers, measuring cylinders, and thermometers correctly to measure length, volume and temperature.
essentialPoints: Length is measured using a ruler with the eye positioned perpendicular to avoid parallax error
Volumes are read at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Temperature is read from a thermometer scale to its stated resolution

nodes.label: AT1: Using a stopwatch/timer for repeated readings
nodes.objective: Use a stopwatch or timer to measure time intervals, taking repeat readings to improve reliability.
essentialPoints: A stopwatch is started and stopped consistently at defined events to measure a time interval
Repeating timings and averaging reduces the effect of random error

nodes.label: AT2: Constructing electrical circuits from circuit diagrams
nodes.objective: Use circuit diagrams to construct and check series and parallel circuits, including ammeters and voltmeters.
essentialPoints: Circuit symbols represent specific components and must be connected as shown in the diagram
Ammeters are connected in series and voltmeters in parallel with the component being measured

nodes.label: AT3: Measuring distance, time and using light gates/motion sensors
nodes.objective: Measure distance and time using appropriate apparatus (including light gates and data loggers where used) to determine motion quantities.
essentialPoints: Distance travelled and corresponding time intervals are measured to calculate speed or acceleration
Light gates/data loggers can measure short time intervals more precisely than manual timing

nodes.label: AT4: Making observations of waves in a ripple tank or with a signal generator
nodes.objective: Use a ripple tank, signal generator, and oscilloscope/microphone to observe and measure wave properties such as frequency and wavelength.
essentialPoints: A ripple tank allows observation of wavefronts to measure wavelength directly
A signal generator and oscilloscope allow frequency and time period of a wave to be determined

nodes.label: AT5: Measuring forces and extension using a newtonmeter and ruler
nodes.objective: Use a newtonmeter to measure force and a ruler to measure the extension of a spring or material under load.
essentialPoints: A newtonmeter (spring balance) measures force directly in newtons
Extension is calculated as the difference between stretched length and natural (unstretched) length

nodes.label: AT6: Using detectors to measure radioactive emissions
nodes.objective: Use a Geiger-Muller tube/counter to detect and measure count rate of radioactive emissions, accounting for background radiation.
essentialPoints: A Geiger-Muller tube detects ionising radiation and a counter records count rate
Background radiation must be measured separately and accounted for when interpreting readings

nodes.label: AT7: Measuring energy changes/transfers using temperature and calorimetry apparatus
nodes.objective: Use thermometers, insulated containers and heaters to measure temperature changes associated with energy transfers.
essentialPoints: Temperature change over time is measured using a thermometer or temperature sensor while a known energy input is applied
Insulation is used to minimise unwanted energy transfer to the surroundings during the measurement

nodes.label: AT8 (physics only): Using ray boxes, mirrors, lenses and protractors for optics
nodes.objective: Use a ray box, protractor, mirrors, and lenses to measure angles of incidence, reflection and refraction, and to trace ray paths.
essentialPoints: A ray box produces a narrow visible beam of light for tracing on paper
A protractor measures angles of incidence, reflection and refraction relative to the normal
